title: Minify replica count: consolidate long-tail models by global routing
idea: Minify how many places each model's weights must be resident: a global router concentrates all traffic for each long-tail model onto the fewest replicas that meet the SLO, and cold models page in from NVMe in under a second.
why: Pinned weight DRAM for fleets of thousands of models falls >=10x, which turns DRAM spend into a scheduling problem.
note: ServerlessLLM-style routing and fast loading known.

title: LLNL ZFP arrays, fixed: lossy compression as a page attribute
idea: ZFP fixed-rate lossy floating-point compression saw low adoption because codes had to be rewritten around compressed-array classes. Put a ZFP engine in the memory controller and let the OS mark pages 'fp64 lossy, 16 bits/value', so unmodified HPC codes get 4x compression with bounded error.
why: ~4x effective DRAM for simulation fields, so HPC nodes need far less DRAM.

title: Fixed-rate ZFP codec in the L2 fill path for simulation arrays
idea: Box: lossy random-access compression × L2 fill/evict path × 4×4×4 float block × fixed 8–16 bits per value × HPC fields. Arrays live in DRAM as fixed-rate ZFP blocks; a cache-side codec decompresses on fill and recompresses on eviction, so code sees plain doubles.
why: HPC mesh size per node is DRAM-bound; 4–8× capacity at error below discretization error.
note: Fixed-rate ZFP in cache fill path is plausible for HPC; hardware ZFP has prior proposals.

title: Vinyl-record pressing: via-programmed mask ROM for frozen model weights
idea: Borrowed from record pressing, where one stamper makes millions of discs: frozen model weights are pressed into 1-transistor mask ROM by a single cheap via/metal mask on a commodity logic wafer (no EUV, no capacitor) stacked under the accelerator, so weights need zero DRAM and zero refresh; a new model version is a new via mask.
why: Removes the weight footprint from DRAM; mask ROM is dense, has zero standby and refresh power, uses mature U.S.-available nodes and needs no capacitor or EUV.

title: Apollo core-rope weaver: frozen weights in via-programmed ROM chiplets
idea: Apollo's flight software was literally woven into core-rope ROM. Production model weights that won't change for a year are mask-programmed into dense, multi-bit, stackable via-ROM chiplets on a mature node and co-packaged beside the accelerator. HBM then holds only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are 50-80% of inference HBM. ROM needs no capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, and it can be made in 28-40 nm US fabs. That frees most HBM for KV cache and attacks capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability.
note: Mature-node ROM cost/bit not clearly below DRAM; win is refresh-free, no EUV, weights out of HBM.

title: Genome Project biologist: open atlas of real memory contents
idea: Biology took off once the genome was sequenced. An opt-in agent samples hashed, entropy-profiled page snapshots (never raw data) from volunteer fleets and publishes a 'memory atlas': the share of zero pages, duplicates, near-duplicates, compressible types, pointer density and cold data by workload. About $800k.
why: Outside three hyperscalers, nobody knows where the reclaimable bytes are. The atlas aims every compression, dedup and tiering effort at the biggest wins, priming 20-40% savings.

title: Americium credit: U.S. tax credit per gigabyte of DRAM avoided
idea: Named for the Americas, a CHIPS-style federal credit pays data-center operators per GB-year of DRAM avoided against a certified baseline (via compression, pooling, reuse) measured by a standard telemetry audit, and federal procurement favors software that publishes bytes-per-transaction figures.
why: Makes memory efficiency a domestic supply lever while the U.S. makes only 1-2% of DRAM; a 15% demand cut equals several fabs' output without $15B of capital (capital, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.
why: If 70% of traffic stays small, giant-model replicas and their HBM drop ~3x.

title: Demoscene 64k coder: neural texture compression plugin for game engines
idea: Demosceners fit whole worlds in 64 KB. An Unreal/Godot plugin encodes each material's texture stack (albedo, normal, roughness and more) into a small latent grid plus a tiny MLP decoded in the shader at sample time, replacing block-compressed mip chains. A 4-person team can build it in 24 months.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game and VR memory. Neural textures give 4-8x over BCn, letting consoles, PCs and headsets ship with less DRAM.
note: NVIDIA NTC already exists; engine plugin is an execution play.

title: 2050 engineer: KV cache stored as per-sequence implicit neural field
idea: A 2050 engineer stores functions, not tables. For each long sequence, a tiny sinusoidal MLP per layer is fitted online to map (position, head) to the K/V vector and refitted incrementally every few hundred tokens, and attention queries this field instead of a table. Exact KV is kept only for the recent window and for outlier tokens the field reconstructs poorly.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory. A 20-50x fit on older tokens would turn 1M-token contexts from hundreds of GB into a few GB. The accuracy risk is high.
note: KV as fitted implicit function could give 20-50x; doubt: K/V vectors are not smooth in position, so fits likely lossy.

title: Rotating nanostructured glass platter streams weights to batch inference
idea: In throughput-oriented batch inference the weight pass is a sequential scan of read-only data, which rotating media serve at the lowest cost per bit. A spinning fused-silica platter with laser-written multilevel nanostructures is read by a 10,000-element VCSEL/photodiode head array (~1 Gb/s each, ~10 Tb/s total), streaming a 70B FP8 model every ~60 ms, amortized over a batch of hundreds of sequences.
why: Weights leave DRAM entirely for batch jobs; the glass medium costs <$0.01/GB and needs no power to retain data.
note: Read-only glass at <$0.01/GB removes weights from DRAM for batch jobs; aligning a 10 Tb/s head array on a spinning platter is the big doubt.

title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are copied 8-64x across a serving pod. One copy plus broadcast (~1.4 TB/s for a 70B fp8 model at 20 steps/s) cuts weight-resident HBM ~Nx, freeing 50-90% of HBM in weight-dominated serving. Attacks the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity.
note: One weight copy streamed per decode step frees most weight-resident HBM; doubt: ~1.4 TB/s optical receive per accelerator and strict lockstep.
